Paul Martin (Essex East: I ask leave, Mr. Speaker, to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the alarming increase in unemployment and the decrease in total employment that occurred in Canada between December and January, as reported in today's release issued by the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of Labour.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East has asked leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the alarming increase in unemployment and the decrease in total employment that occurred in Canada between December and January, as reported in today's release issued by the dominion bureau of statistics.
The question that has to be decided by the Chair-the only question the Chair has to decide-is the question of the urgency of debate. The importance of this matter to the country or to parliament is not what I have to consider, but rather the opportunities there are to discuss the subject matter and whether this is the type of suddenly arising urgent matter which would warrant an interruption of the ordinary routine of business so that it might be discussed.
If I had serious doubts about the question of urgency I would be glad to hear the hon. member for Essex East and other hon. members, but it seems to me that in line with decisions I have made previously on this general question, particularly at a time when the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne had not been concluded, it would be very difficult to make out a case of urgency for any matter of this kind.
I recall that during the last session while the throne speech debate was in progress, reference was made to the question of unemployment. In fact it was the subject of continuous discussion in parliament throughout
the whole session. I think as long as unemployment exists in substantial proportions it will be a subject of discussion in this parliament.
In support of what I have said I offer the following citations. The first is from Beau-chesne's fourth edition, at page 90, citation 100, paragraph 3:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
On page 91 there is reference to the type of discussion for which the rule might be invoked which I think is worth repeating to the house. I begin on page 91 about half way down the page. The quotation refers to a motion to discuss the neglect of the government to take measures for the relief of agricultural depression. This is what is said by the learned author:
What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs. But I do not think it was contemplated-if the house will allow me to state my views-that a question of very wide scope, which would demand legislation to deal with it in any effective manner, should be the subject of discussion on a motion for the adjournment of the house, because, if that was so, we might have repeated motions made by the opposition of the day, not so much in the direction of censuring the government for action which had been taken or not taken, for bringing to notice some grievance demanding instant remedy, as in the direction of wishing to introduce legislation on some particular subject. That is not the purpose of the standing order of 1882, and would, I think, cut at the root of the order."
The only factor which I can see in the hon. member's request which denotes a change of state is that the latest figures of total employment and unemployment are different from those of the preceding period. They suggest a change in trend or proportions the details of which have not been mentioned by the hon. member. But accepting that there is a substantial change as indicated by the figures, then it seems to me the whole subject is one which has already been discussed this session in part in some of the debates, and for which there will be opportunity for discussion as soon as the throne speech debate is resumed.
Therefore my disposition is to rule out this motion as not being within the rule, basically on the ground that the test of urgency of debate has not been satisfied but aso on the

ground which I stated previously, that relating to the breadth and character of the problem.

speechtext:
First I should like to observe that there has been no more loyal member of the international monetary fund than Canada. This country has been a member of the fund


since it was established, and has strongly supported the activities of the fund in promoting freedom of payments in support of world trade. We supported the increase several years ago in the resources of the fund, and indeed took down a very substantial subscription in that respect. We have also taken part in the recent movement to enlarge the reserves available to the fund, and certain members of it, on a stand-by basis.
The relationship of the Canadian dollar to the United States dollar is not a new matter by any means. There was an attempt made a decade ago, indeed two separate attempts, to maintain the Canadian dollar at a fixed relationship to the United States dollar, at one time on a 90 cents basis and another time on a 100 cents basis, but these attempts had to be abandoned. There has been no fixed and firm relationship maintained between these two currencies over the past decade, so that the position which has obtained since June 20 last is not a new one in kind at all. It is simply a movement of the Canadian dollar to a discount position in terms of the United States dollar, whereas previously it had been in a premium position in relation to the United States dollar. Under the articles of the fund there has been no change in that respect.
I have already stated in this house that I said at the annual meeting of the governors of the fund at Vienna in September that the policy of the government is taken in the light of the circumstances affecting Canada's balance of payments position, so that it is quite clearly understandable. It is understood, I think, by all members of the fund, that it is not undertaken with a view to doing hurt or harm to the interests of any country in the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-63, respecting the construction of a line of railway in the province of Alberta by Canadian National Railway Company from Whitecourt, Alberta, in a westerly direction for a distance of approximately 23.2 miles to the property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as the title of the bill indicates, authority is being sought to enable Canadian National Railway Company to build a 23 mile branch line from Whitecourt, Alberta, as an extension of the railway's Sangudo subdivision, which now terminates at that point.
This new branch line would cross the McLeod river at Whitecourt and proceed in a westerly direction, generally following the grade of the Peace river branch, originally proposed to be constructed in 1924 but never finally completed, to the property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation in the Windfall gas field area, where a plant to produce sulphur from natural gas is now being constructed. The cost to construct the railway line is estimated at $2,300,000 or $99,138 per mile.
An agreement has been concluded between the railway company and Texas Gulf Sulphur Company, wherein a guarantee is given that the industry will ship a minimum tonnage of sulphur over the branch line for 25 years, and that appropriate penalties will be paid if at any period during that term shipments fall below the minimum volume agreed to. In addition, the industry has agreed to make a substantial cash contribution toward the cost of construction of the
line which, of course, reduces the amount which will need to be provided under the terms of the bill.
The production of sulphur from natural gas in Canada is a relatively new development, and interest in it arises from the fact that the reserves of large producers of elemental sulphur in the southern United States are now showing signs of exhaustion. The present proposal is the result of negotiations between Texas Gulf Sulphur Company and Canadian National Railways respecting transportation service to a sulphur recovery plant in the Windfall gas field area, where the natural gas contains substantial amounts of sulphur. The initial output from this plant is estimated at 237,000 long tons annually. Production is expected to increase to 614,000 long tons per year by 1972, and to continue at about that rate until the gas reserves are exhausted. The life of the field is estimated at around 25 years.
The prospective traffic on the proposed line would consist mainly of sulphur, estimated to amount to a total of 500,000 long tons in the first five years, increasing to an indicated maximum rate of around
400,000	long tons per year. It is expected that the sulphur will move mainly to Vancouver for export. Other traffic would consist of chemicals and other supplies for operation of the sulphur recovery plant, pipe and other materials involved in any new developments in the field, and possibly pulpwood.
As I said when I spoke on the resolution preceding the bill, this project deserves encouragement as one which should improve the net position of the Canadian National and at the same time contribute to the development of the area concerned. I mentioned also the urgency associated with the passage of this legislation, arising out of the fact that the industry has requested rail service not later than March 1, 1963, and that in order to meet this date the railway must construct the piers and abutments of the bridge over the McLeod river near White-court at low water, during the present winter season. Therefore a start must be made on these piers and abutments as soon as possible.
The proposal commends itself as one which will assist in developing markets for these resources Of the country, and is sound from an economic standpoint.
In view of the urgency of this project, and because there is every reason to avoid delay which might jeopardize the whole project, I intend to request that this bill be considered by the committee of the whole instead of referring it to the standing committee on

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no change in our position so far as approval of this bill is concerned. I believe the position of the official opposition was made quite clear in the remarks I made yesterday. There are, however, some questions that remain unanswered from yesterday as well as others that arise from the statement the minister has just made.
One of the questions I put to the minister yesterday concerned a comparison of the cost per mile of this railway with that of other railways in the immediate or adjacent area. Apparently the minister overlooked answering that.
The minister has stated that an agreement has been entered into between the Texas Gulf Sulphur Company and Canadian National Railways for a period of 25 years for the movement of a certain amount of sulphur over the line. I do not think the minister has given the house sufficient information to warrant approval in connection with that matter. I asked yesterday for the production of the agreement, and the minister said that could not be done. I then asked for a summary of the terms of the agreement, because I did not think we had received sufficient detail, and today the minister engaged in what was almost a repetition of what was said yesterday. I think the house should know who the Texas Gulf Sulphur Company is. Is it a subsidiary of the Pan American Petroleum Corporation to whose property this railway is being built? I believe the house would be interested in knowing something of the background of this corporation.
Then the minister referred to the prospective traffic for the first five years of 500,000 long tons. Can the minister give some indication of the freight rate at which the movement will take place? Then again it was indicated that most of this sulphur, if not all of it, would be sent to Vancouver for export. Is any of it going to be used for
Canadian National Railways domestic purposes in Canada? Is there a demand for this product for industrial purposes in our own country? Can the minister give some idea of what the other traffic is likely to amount to? He referred to chemicals, pulpwood and other commodities of that kind. What is the percentage of that traffic over the line as compared with the sulphur, which unquestionably is the most important traffic?
Then as to the urgency may I say this. I believe the minister put his case yesterday, as we did also. However, there is one thing I must bring to the attention of the minister, namely the fact that he intends to move that this legislation be referred to the committee of the whole. I must bring to his attention the fact that this may be the only occasion on which a precedent such as this has been followed. I may be mistaken. It is possible that when I occupied the position he now holds there may have been cases in which this was done, but I doubt it very much. In any event, in answer to a question of mine yesterday the minister made it quite clear, that this matter would be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. As reported at page 772 of Hansard of February 12, 1962 the minister had this to say in answer to a question I put to him earlier:
The hon. member for Laurier has pointed out that in my remarks on the resolution I did not state I intended to ask that the Whitecourt bill_
That is the one now under consideration.
-be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I intended to do that on second reading. I can assure the hon. member now that we definitely intend to refer this bill to the committee.
I think the minister owes the house an explanation as to why, overnight, he has changed his mind and now asks that this matter be referred to the committee of the whole. I must tell the minister that we are going to oppose this suggestion with all our might. Whether or not there is urgency, it has been the practice of this house to refer matters of this kind to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines so that we can have the officers before us and can inquire from them as to the details of the agreement.
The minister says he cannot give the agreement. We have not a summary of the agreement, but only some of the details. Now the matter is to be referred to the committee of the whole, where we certainly will not be in a position to examine the officers. That procedure is contrary to the whole tradition of parliament, and I from this side of the house must object to it and protest as strongly as possible.

Canadian National Railways
I hope the minister will come back to his original idea of referring the matter to the standing committee. We on this side of the house will co-operate with the minister in establishing the standing committee so the officers can come forward. I think it would be a derogation from the rights of parliament to ask the committee of the whole to deal with a matter of this importance. Even though there is urgency for the construction of the piers, as I am prepared to admit, the urgency certainly is not such that we cannot have before the railway committee a discussion of the merits of the agreement.
I repeat what I said yesterday, namely that on the principle of the bill or on the merits of the legislation we are prepared to support it, as it is a project which will assist in the development of the resources of one province and incidentally in the development of our country as a whole. However, we cannot consent or agree to the suggestion made by the minister that the matter be referred to the committee of the whole for discussion.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier has stated quite strongly his party's objections to putting this legislation through the committee of the whole rather than through the regular channel, namely the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I feel just as strongly about the matter, though perhaps for somewhat different reasons. In order to make my point I turn to two practical examples rather than to the infringement of parliamentary rights, although I agree with him on that matter.
In our own region we have two situations which were caused by extensions in C.N.R. facilities in the last decade or so and which are very much up in the air now. One of the reasons for the situations happens to be that not enough information was garnered at the launching of the enterprise. At the present time we have a very bitter debate going on between the iron mines in Steep Rock which are shipping out of Atikokan to Port Arthur on the C.N.R., over the freight rates that are being charged. The argument being made by the C.N.R. is that in terms of volume the mines have not lived up to the agreement that was entered into some years ago, and that therefore it has been necessary to raise the rates. On the other hand the mines are arguing that this is a punitive measure which is going to cause them a great deal of trouble.
Without taking sides on the merits of the matter-though I must admit that my sympathies are with the local agency rather than with the national one-I may say it is quite
[Mr. Chevrler.)

apparent that there is a great deal of misunderstanding about the original agreement. Here in the house the minister says he cannot give the details because to do so would be tough on the competitive position of the C.N.R. I might point out that the Atikokan situation is very much like this one. At Atikokan there was no real alternative means of transportation other than the Canadian National Railways, and I understand the same situation exists in this case. I fail to see that the excuse or the reason given by the minister stands up.
The other example I should like to bring to the minister's attention with regard to the need to examine branch lines closely is one I will take from my own area, where we had a line built in to Manitouwadge a number of years ago. The discovery really got under way in 1953. "What happened there was that both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway built lines into the mine, and at the present time neither railway has enough traffic really to be remunerative. We have the spectacle of an additional branch line in the area.
Here again it seems to me in retrospect that parliament bore a responsibility for failing to go into the nature of the agreement existing between the Canadian National Railways and the mining corporation. These are two examples from my own area that lead me to believe we need the opportunity to examine and cross-examine the officials concerned. We cannot do that in the committee of the whole.
The third argument that I would bring to the minister in this regard relates to something which is becoming the theme in transportation today in Canada and which has been echoed by the royal commission on transportation. I refer to the theme that the railways must get out of the branch line business. In any case in which a branch line is being abandoned I understand that all kinds of opportunities are given to the public in the areas concerned to come forward and express their views or their arguments pro and con. I may say that most of them will be con.
In a situation like this, which underlines the uneconomic nature of so many of the branch lines the railways built, it seems to me we need to be almost unnaturally vigilant in any case in which the Canadian National Railway in particular is getting into further branch lines. I can assure the minister that I am not exaggerating my doubts when I say that with regard to this particular enterprise, which on the face of the minister's

explanation is a good one, I will feel much happier if we have the opportunity to deal with the matter in a committee.
Now the minister suggested that the urgency is so great that we cannot take time to refer the bill to a standing committee. Surely this committee could meet on Thursday morning and study this particular bill, or early next week at the latest. I cannot see that a delay of from three to five days could possibly be crucial in the building of only some 20-odd miles of track. For these reasons we will object to and if necessary vote against second reading of this bill, if we are not going to have an opportunity of examining it in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
I appreciate the fact that I did not hear the explanation of the regional aspects of this rail project given by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. I should like to congratulate him and the other members from Alberta upon having, in connection with their oil industry, so many wonderful opportunities for expansion. The views I have expressed about the desirability of sending this measure to a standing committee are not to be regarded as an attempt to block the advantages of this enterprise to the area in Alberta which the hon. member represents.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
I should like to add a few words to what I said yesterday on this measure at the resolution stage. I think I could echo the minister's request for speed, because there is real urgency in getting the piers built across the McLeod river. The McLeod river is a relatively short, swift, mountain river which flows into the Athabasca at the town of Whitecourt. In order to get the heavy equipment into the area it will be necessary to have the bridge built first. This is the important consideration. The bridge will have to be built before the equipment to build the line can be taken farther into the country.
It is particularly important that these abutments and piers be put in place this winter. We have approximately only a month left in which to complete this work. I appreciate the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, but five days may make quite a bit of difference in getting the concrete poured. Each day is going to become extremely important in building these piers.
There is another factor that is of importance. As I said, the town of Whitecourt is a boom area and there has been a large influx of workers awaiting the start of construction on the newsprint plant, awaiting the start of
Canadian National Railways construction on the railway and looking for jobs in connection with gas extraction. There is a surplus of manpower there at the moment, so if we could get this bill passed we could get these men started to work on the bridge and then clearing the line. These two factors are of importance when we consider the urgency for getting started on the bridge.
There is one other matter I should like to refer to, and that is the sulphur which was mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier. We will be using some of this sulphur locally in the pulp mill, and we expect there will be a local demand for sulphur as well. There is a market for Alberta sulphur in British Columbia, but a large volume of the sulphur will either have to be exported or moved to Ontario. As I said yesterday, the total usage of sulphur in Canada is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 600,000 tons a year. Within about five years this one plant will be producing that much. We also hope, particularly in the farm areas I represent, that some of this sulphur will be more easily available for use as fertilizer, because it has been shown that elemental sulphur is very beneficial on the grey wood soils of Alberta. We are hopeful that this sulphur will be used in the chemical complex which is now being established around Edmonton. Perhaps a further chemical industry will be established, and we would hope it might be decentralized out of Edmonton as a result of the development at White-court.
It is for these reasons, and the fact that this development is at the moment marking time, that I sincerely ask the house to consider giving quick passage to this bill. There is one other point I should like to make with regard to divulging the details of the agreement. I believe I recall that last year a private bill was introduced to grant the Canadian Pacific Railway permission to build eight miles of track into a similar plant at Rimbey, Alberta. The Canadian National is concerned because there are more than 14 of these plants in Alberta. They are not all owned by the same people, and it is becoming a very competitive business. While it is true that the Canadian National is the only railway in the immediate area, I think it becomes apparent that the sulphur company will be concerned if the complete arrangements are divulged, because this will weaken their competitive position in the sulphur industry of Alberta.
I just bring to the attention of the house the fact that last year the Canadian Pacific requested permission to build an identical extension to a plant at Rimbey, Alberta. I am
814	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways sure they were not required to reveal all the details of the agreement with British American Oil at that time, so it would be putting Canadian National in an unfair position, as well as the Texas Gulf Sulphur Company, to ask them to reveal the details of the agreement now.
In conclusion I would say that while I appreciate the fact that some of our branch line building in Canada has not been well directed, I am sure that the tonnage and the contributions made by the company will mean that at the end of 25 years railway construction costs will have been paid off and the line will be showing a reasonable profit. It seems to me that this is a reasonable bill. Again I ask the house to consider the urgency for constructing the bridge across the McLeod river. This has to be done within the next month, and the days do count in this regard.

speechtext:
I am sure all of us are influenced strongly by the very sensible considerations that have been advanced by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, who is properly concerned that this project should get under way just as quickly as possible. If there were any risk of any real delay, any likelihood of any real delay in the procedure we suggest, I think we would have to give some consideration to the feelings which the hon. member has expressed. However, I think the house should bear this fact in mind, that the debate on the address was adjourned on January 25 and that it has not been resumed on February 13. If we had proceeded in the normal way this session and had gone right on, the debate on the address would have been finished by February 1, two weeks ago. This bill could then have been given priority over every other piece of legislation. It could have been disposed of very quickly and could have been on the statute books before this. So, if there has been any delay, the delay cannot be blamed on the opposition. It is the customary bad management of the sessional affairs by the government.
Apparently the government had some frantic reasons for departing from the normal procedure in parliament, some frantic reasons for interrupting the business of the house which the Prime Minister told us was going to be interrupted for only two measures but, as has occurred, it has been interrupted since for over a week. The business of the house could have proceeded until the four days of debate on the address had been completed, without injury to anyone and this bill could then have been given priority.


Even now, as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) pointed out very cogently, there is no reason why the committee should not be set up.
I am speaking without having consulted my hon. friend from Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) but I am sure we on our part would be prepared to have a motion made and disposed of at once to set up the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, so that it could meet on Thursday morning and dispose of this matter then. It seems to me that would not be diffcult but it also seems to me, in view of what the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Port Arthur have said, we have a duty in this house, on both sides of the house but particularly on the opposition side, to scrutinize all these railway bills at a time when the royal commission appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite is suggesting that hundreds of miles of railways be torn up all over the country.
When we are being asked to build new branch lines it is our duty to see that these lines are warranted, and not take them on faith from the government. I am not questioning the good faith of the government when I say this. I am just saying that is the proper way to do it, and the Minister of Transport evidently thought so last night because his language was quite categorical, as reported at page 772 of Hansard. It would not seem to me that any new consideration has developed overnight, unless some of the suspicions of my hon. friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin) are correct.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is undoubtedly an honour for me to sponsor today a bill the purpose of which is to promote the industrial and commercial development of one of the most picturesque areas of the province of Quebec, the Gaspe peninsula. Most members of the house are familiar with that region and all will agree with me that it is a most interesting part of our country, not only as a tourist attraction but also because of its population whose distinctive features have always appealed to other Canadians.
Indeed, Gaspe, that rugged part of our country, was settled by pioneers several hundred years ago. The people of the Gaspe peninsula have lived through rather difficult
times, quite often without other means of survival than fishing and a little wood-cutting, and their activities have always been hampered by the lack of transportation facilities. Yet, both the federal and provincial governments were often urged to find means of ensuring the economic survival of that part of our country so that its people would enjoy the same standard of living as the rest of Canada.
The problem of transportation in general was brought to the public's attention in the lower St. Lawrence district and the Gaspe peninsula many years ago. More recently, in the past ten years, the chambers of commerce, the municipal councils, the economic planning councils, all kinds of associations and all those who are concerned with the particular problems of that area, have given thorough consideration to the problems of transportation within the peninsula and between Gaspe and the other Canadian centres.
Renowned experts like Mr. Pierre Camu and Dr. Huet Massue have prepared extensive reports on that problem in eastern Quebec. Those documents have shown among other things that the lack of railway facilities in the Gaspe peninsula, is an obstacle to the development of an area which has always suffered from the fact that it is traditionally far from markets.
The economic future of the lower St. Lawrence district and of the Gaspe peninsula is directly related to the means of transportation available. The present government appreciates the magnitude of the problem and that is why it has taken bold and courageous action in that field. It did not merely make promises, it took initiatives: harbour improvements, new "roll on roll off" ferry services, year-round navigation between both shores of the St. Lawrence. In the same spirit, it now seeks the house's approval of a bill which would earmark $14 million for the construction of a new railway between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts.
A moment ago, I spoke of the ferry service we provided in that part of the lower St. Lawrence district.
The geographical location of the Gaspe peninsula has tragical effects. In fact, Gaspe is right in front of one of the richest districts in Canada, perhaps in the whole world; several billions of dollars are being spent on development in that area which is but some ten miles from Gaspe. That was the situation in the Gaspe peninsula; with the years it became a depressed area and, as usual, the people started moving out.
818	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways
Our government is convinced that if transportation facilities are multiplied between Gaspe and the rest of Canada, and especially through a ferry service between the peninsula and the north shore, the people will start moving back to Gaspe which was settled over 300 years ago whereas the north shore was opened up on a large scale only in the past fifteen years.
The government hopes that this will bring about an exchange of population between the two shores of the St. Lawrence, which should further the development of the Gaspe peninsula.
As I pointed out earlier, the big problem in the Gaspe peninsula is one of transportation, and I am convinced that this measure which I have the privilege of introducing in this house today will be another factor in allowing the people of this area to attain the same economic level as the rest of the country.
There already is a line of some 40 miles in length between Mont Joli and Matane and, with the addition of the projected line, this will mean that the area extending from Mont Joli to Ste. Anne des Monts will be served by a railway on a distance of some 100 miles. Moreover, the population to be served by this railway, or directly concerned with this bill, exceeds 100,000.
Already, some mining companies have indicated that the extension of the line to Ste. Anne des Monts will enable them to carry out their development projects. One such case is that of a subsidiary of the East Sullivan Mines Ltd. I have seen correspondence in which officials of this well known company have indicated that, if the area in which they own properties could be joined to Ste. Anne des Monts, they would be in a position to develop them economically.
It may also be inferred that several other mining companies were only waiting for adequate means of transportation before increasing their mining operations.
Ever since the development of the Murdoch-ville mine started, the people of the Gaspe peninsula have been hopeful because that very rugged country contains huge mineral deposits.
That is why the government submits today to the consideration of this house a bill which will provide for the development, on a sound basis, of all those mineral deposits and of the other natural resources of Gaspe such as wood and wood products. I have no doubt that the construction of this railway line will be conducive to the solution of the economic problems of that region.


I also know that one of the most important pulp and paper companies in the province of Quebec has always wanted the extension of that railway line to Ste. Anne des Monts because in the forests of the Gaspe peninsula lie almost unlimited resources. Yet, in recent years, we have witnessed the tragedy of a people living on a quite scant income only a few miles in the interior of a peninsula which has boundless forests that could not be developed on a sound basis because of the lack of transportation.
The bill under discussion provides for the construction and the operation of a railway line, from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts, in the constituencies of Matane and Gaspe. That region of the Gaspe peninsula has been for some time the proposed site for a railway; but the project was never carried out. This construction will therefore be an effort or rather a development project to improve the economy of that region, to give the lumber industry easier access to the markets and to promote the development of mines and other resources in that part of the Gaspe peninsula by providing direct transportation by rail. The possible traffic, without taking into account future mining developments, would be made up of pulpwood, shavings, lumber, gasoline, oil and building materials and goods in general.
In view of the fact that this is a development project, the procedure adopted will be as follows: the Canadian National Railways will build the line on behalf of the government; the company will operate and maintain that line on the same basis. The surplus in revenue from this line will be given over to the government; on the other hand, any deficit suffered by the Canadian National Railways will be made good. This line will be linked to the main line of the Canadian National Railways through the Canada Gulf Terminal line. The line will cover a distance of approximately 57 miles and cost approximately $14 millions.
Mr. Chairman, as the house can see, this is a development railway, a railway for the development of natural resources which, at the present time, are untapped.
We are convinced that the future will prove right those who have advocated that project, the people of the Gaspe peninsula who have been asking for that railway for years, and the government which puts its faith in the people of the Gaspe peninsula, while promoting the economic development of Canada and, in particular, of the province of Quebec and that region of the province.

Some hon. members may express doubts as to the advisability of constructing that line now instead of next year but I think that we must have vision and construct right now this development railway which will not only provide for the development of natural resources in the Gaspe peninsula but will also offer to its people who have always lacked adequate transportation an opportunity to ship their products without paying prohibitive transport rates. This railway will also enable them to compete in the domestic market.
Mr. Chairman, as I mentioned a moment ago, this is a development railway. It is a railway which is to be built and operated by the C.N.R. That is why I intend during the debate on second reading, to table the draft contract between the government and the Canadian National Railways.
Therefore, it gives me pleasure, Mr. Chairman, to commend this resolution to the approval of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I followed closely the statement of the minister on the construction of a railway line between Ma-tane and Ste. Anne des Monts.
During the course of his remarks he told us that the object of this line is to develop the Gaspe area which has suffered for many long years from a lack of transportation. He told us the construction of this line was intended to promote industrial, and commercial development in that area of the Gaspe peninsula.
We, who are sitting on this side of the house, are in agreement with what the minister said, and consequently we intend to support the measure he introduced today.
It is not the first time that reference is being made to the construction of a railroad in the Gaspe peninsula. Indeed, the minister said himself that many are those who have promoted such a project.
It is obvious that the means of transportation in that area are of concern to all those who have at heart the development of the Gaspe area. I do not refer exclusively to individuals and business firms, to corporations and associations, but to several others who, for many years, have made representations in favour of such a project.
The minister referred in particular to the study of the matter made by Messrs. Pierre Camu and Huet Massue. So, I should like to read into the record some of the recommendations made by Mr. Pierre Camu in his report entitled "Transportation Problems in
Canadian National Railways the Lower St. Lawrence Area", which was submitted by the lower St. Lawrence council on economic planning in 1960.
The minister, I am sure, will have no objection to my reading into the record some recommendations concerning not only the railroad, but all the subjects to which he referred, including the ferries and other means of transportation between both shores of the St. Lawrence.
I do not propose to read into the record all of what Mr. Camu recommends. But it seems to me that some of his recommendations should be brought to the attention of the house.
In the conclusion of that report, which may be found on page 91, we read the following: Recommendations and suggestions
1.	About the port area Riviere du Loup-Gros Cacouna, we believe that this area could attract a potential traffic of more than 1,227,000 tons from an hinterland including the counties of Riviere du Loup, Temiscouata and Kamouraska, the northeastern part of New Brunswick and the northeastern part of the state of Maine. To handle such a traffic, adequate port facilities are required to accommodate at the same time at least two sea-going vessels of three thousand gross tons; a shed 300 feet long by 50 feet wide must also be provided, as well as a railroad and necessary wharves for a ferry. Consideration should perhaps be given to choosing another site for the present wharf at Riviere du Loup. The Gros Cacouna site would seem to be the most appropriate.
2.	In order to improve the port of Matane, the possibility of changing the course of the mouth of the river could be considered; it would then be easier to drag the basin and maintain water at an adequate level. Another solution would consist in extending the pier or to construct a submerged pier to hold back alluvial deposits at the port entrance.
I shall skip the third recommendation, which deals with a purely provincial matter.
4.	To maintain and develop marketing and trade with the north shore, we suggest the establishment of three ferry services: between Riviere du Loup or Gros Cacouna and Tadoussac; between Rimouski and Pointe au Pere and Baie Comeau; and between Matane and Godbout. We recommend the use of ferry boats which can navigate through ice floes and carry, each trip, a few trailer trucks and one or two buses.
5.	We contemplate the possibility of grain elevators, of the type built at Baie Comeau and designed for the same purpose, being erected in the harbours of the area.
Another possibility would be, especially in winter, to accentuate the national character of the lower St. Lawrence ports, to make them gateways of Canadian trade.
6.	The matter of grants to shipping companies should be re-examined by both governments, the Quebec government and the federal government.
A total of $241,000 is paid annually to the shipping companies servicing the lower St. Lawrence. That is not much compared to what is paid elsewhere for so-called "essential" services. We believe that the economic planning council for the lower St. Lawrence is entitled to know whether the services

Canadian National Railways
offered by the companies are consistent with the intent and the letter of the acts governing the conditions of payment of the grants.
I skip recommendation 7 and pass on to 8 which reads as follows:
8.	We believe that the introduction of the piggyback service would be beneficial to the economy of the lower St. Lawrence region and that it should be given a try, providing that the truckers can drive overnight the full distance between Mont Joli and Montreal, either way, all year round.
9.	The Canada and Gulf Terminal Railway should be taken over by the Canadian National Railways as soon as possible.
Finally:
12. The trucking companies are up against a competition they call unfair from the railways. As a matter of fact, in that part of Quebec, the trucking companies that operate between various cities charge rates lower than those of the other companies in the province, in order to compete with the rates set by the railways whose operating deficits are made up through grants at the end of the year. And yet, the trucking companies in the area pay the same taxes, buy the same permits, etc., as similar companies elsewhere in the province.
The provincial government should increase the maximum permissible load from 50,000 to 60,000 pounds, and the provincial transport commission should allow direct transportation, by the same carrier, of goods shipped from one city to another in the area.
15.	The establishment of railcar services between Riviere du Loup and Matane, Riviere du Loup and Edmunston and Mont Joli and Campbellton-Dal-housie should be requested.
16.	The Mont Joli airport should become the regional airport of the lower St. Lawrence.
17.	As for passenger traffic, the aims of the economic council of the lower St. Lawrence should be: (1) to see to it that the highway system is improved; (2) to make suggestions to the department of roads as to what is felt desirable for the years to come; (3) to study and analyse the timetables of the railway, bus and air line companies, with a view to improving and facilitating movements within the area, and between that area and surrounding areas.
I wanted to bring to the attention of this house the careful study carried out by Dr. Camu, at the time director of research in the department of commerce of Laval university, who is now, as it is generally known, vice president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. When he prepared this brief and made those recommendations, he had studied the whole question of transportation in the lower St. Lawrence district.
Thus, as far as the railway legislation mentioned by the minister, and which is now before the house is concerned, we should seriously consider all suggestions made by an expert in this matter, some of which can be approved by the federal government and the Department of Transport, while others are under provincial jurisdiction.
The minister told us that the railway will go from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts. He also stated that a crown corporation-I assume he meant the C.N.R.-would be responsible for building and operating the

railway and that, if there were any deficits, they would also be covered by that crown company, while, in the case of a surplus, the company would benefit.
I think it is also important to know what will become of the gap between Matane and Mont Joli, where the Canada and Gulf Terminal Railway operates, which is owned neither by the federal government nor by an agent of the crown, but by some other entity. As the government did not expropriate that railway, it is neither the owner nor, if I am not mistaken, does it have a right of way on that line. Would the minister tell us what arrangements will be made with the owners of the Canada and Gulf Terminal to enable the C.N.R. to extend its track to Ste. Anne des Monts?
Nor did the minister tell us whether that 57 mile railway line will be extended by 44 miles, and by a further 46 miles to the site of the Gaspe Copper Mine, or whether it will be extended by 44 miles plus 14 miles to the Federal Metal Corporation, those companies being copper mining developments.
The minister said that there would be transportation facilities for the ore from those mines. Will those facilities follow the recommendations made by Mr. Camu? For instance, will there be any day-lines or piggy-back service from those mines to Ste. Anne des Monts?
I think the house wants to have some idea of the government's intention in this respect.
Now, the minister talked about the great benefits to our industry and our trade which will result from the construction of this railway. There is no doubt about that. But I also ask the minister the following question: could he not have done the same thing he did in the case of this railway for an air line operating in the lower St. Lawrence, the Quebecair company. The minister is surely aware of the fact that this company has faced rather serious difficulties for some time, and the government had a good opportunity to offer such help. I do not intend for one moment to throw any blame on the minister himself because, from the reply he gave to a question I put in this house, it appears that it is the government which has not deemed proper, either through the air transport board or through a submission to the treasury board, to allow a grant or a payment to this air line for its winter operations.
Perhaps the minister, when replying to our remarks, could tell us how it is that, with regard to this transportation system, it has not been possible to provide assistance. Could he tell us more specifically whether or not that railway, which is intended of

course for the development of the area, is not granted more or less as a compensation for having refused to assist the air line?
Mr. Chairman, I have said enough for the time being. We shall wholeheartedly support the proposed construction of that railroad which will extend 57 miles. We shall support it because we believe it is for the industrial and commercial development of the lower St. Lawrence area, which is now developing not only on account of the mines, referred to by the minister, but also on account of the iron ore deposits of the north shore, the development of which has been rendered possible, to a great extent, by the St. Lawrence seaway.
It is not impossible that with the years that line which will soon be constructed may serve to supplement other means of transportation which have been established in that area by previous governments.
For all those reasons, the opposition will not only be pleased, but will consider it a duty, to support the resolution.

I have been particularly interested in this measure because I noted, in reviewing the hearings of the royal commission on transportation, there was a certain sense of loss, or perhaps it would be better described as a feeling on the part of the Quebec government at the time the hearings were held that Quebec had not had its fair share of railway development in the twentieth century. The Quebec provincial brief was presented by Daniel Johnson, who I understand is now the leader of the opposition but at that time was the minister in charge of the department of the Quebec government that had the responsibility for making the presentation to the royal commission.
In a number of places he argues that from 1920 to 1958 in particular, while development lines were being pursued in other parts of the country, Quebec was going short, and that this particularly applied to lines of the Canadian National Railways. His actual words appear at page 7692 of the transcript of the hearing, where he said:
It should be pointed out that Quebec got the least increase of all the provinces of Canada during these many years. It may be pointed out to us that we must take into consideration the location of the network with regard to the geographic location of the population, that we have less miles of railway than the other provinces of Canada with regard to their population, but that the network is better situated, performs better, carries more. In brief, that it is efficient. The problem, as we see it, must be related to the role that the railway has played and will play in the development of a territory or region and we think that the regions which are not now served or served poorly in Quebec, would have benefited considerably and would have gained
Canadian National Railways more by a more concentrated network, especially when the railway favours the development of the natural resources of the region.
Then, Mr. Johnson goes on to indicate the areas in Quebec which he feels, and the Quebec government at the time felt, should have railway extensions. The first one was from Mont Laurier to Maniwaki; the second, from Mont Laurier to Senneterre; the third, was Dolbeau and Baie Comeau, Port Cartier and Seven Islands; the fourth, Chicoutimi and Tadoussac-Baie Comeau-Port Cartier and Seven Islands; the fifth, Gaspe and Matane, along the St. Lawrence; sixth, La Malbaie and Tadoussac, and around the Saguenay towards Seven Islands; seventh, Angliers and Rouyn-Noranda.
Now, the government apparently has decided that this particular line has priority over the others that were indicated as meriting development on the part of the Canadian National Railways. I would hope that in committee we could expect to get an explanation as to why this particular line has been given priority. I am not being critical, but since suggestions have been made that there are eight possible lines that should be pursued and one has been chosen, we will want to know the reason this particular line has priority, especially in view of the fact there is not the usual economic activity directly associated with this line such as existed in connection with the extensions that were put into Chibougamau or the one we are planning into Alberta in connection with the sulphur development.
I would hope, for that reason, when the minister is giving his explanation or perhaps when the bill is before the committee, we could be told why this particular line was chosen. We must honestly admit that we know very little about the potentialities of that particular region of the country. I again point out that the chamber of commerce representing Gaspe appeared before the royal commission on transportation. I have gone through their brief and their cross-examination, but I cannot find any indication of a particularly enthusiastic investigation of this particular line, in the sense that other regional groups who came to the hearings in Quebec made strong pleas. For example, the delegation from Lake St. John region and the other group from Abitibi made very strong representations about branch line development. Since the chamber of commerce from Gaspe did not do more than raise the question, then the question arises in my mind, why was this particular line given priority over the other requests?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-13, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill, an act to amend the Criminal Code, is identical in every way with a bill introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was a distinguished member of the opposition. I introduce this bill for the very same reasons that he introduced his, and with the same objectives.
The purpose of this bill is to make it a criminal offence for every owner, lessee or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, saw mill or other plant or works, or any other person to discharge or throw or allow to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water any part of which is interprovincial or which flows into any interprovincial water, which has the effect of endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public.
Anyone committing an offence under this amendment would be liable to a fine of $25,000 for a first offence and $50,000 for a second offence, or would be guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction. I realize the scope of this bill is somewhat limited in extent, but I do think it is one step we can take to deal with the growing problem of pollution. It would indicate that this house is willing to amend federal legislation to exercise the authority of the federal parliament in doing what can be done to prevent this growing and increasingly dangerous nuisance.
I might say that I have always taken an interest in the question of conservation of natural resources, particularly with respect to the maintenance of the pure state of our rivers, lakes, streams and other waters. Personally I am in the happy position of living a great number of miles from my nearest neighbour and my domestic and irrigation water comes from a snow capped mountain. So far as I can anticipate, I shall not suffer from any menace of pollution from the action of any other human being. On that account I am particularly concerned with the problem as it faces Canadians in more densely populated portions of Canada and possibly am
[The Chairman.]
more horrified than some who live under these conditions, particularly in Ontario, when I see beautiful rivers polluted by sewage and industrial waste, with little being done to correct the situation throughout the years.
This problem is of growing concern to an increasing number of Canadians. I recognize that from the interest taken in it by municipal authorities, provincial authorities, and other local groups, organizations and agencies. It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that more people are becoming increasingly interested in the problem.
In my constituency the people are fortunate in so far as most of them live on the great Columbia river and the great Kootenay river or some of its tributaries. Up to recent days they have been free from the menace of pollution; but with industrial expansion they are becoming aware of the possibility of pollution in future, and are very anxious to do all they can to maintain the purity of the water they have enjoyed throughout the years. They are anxious to mantain its purity for domestic purposes and also for the continued propagation of the large fish population which is to be found in the lakes there. They are very anxious that action be taken before it is too late, before we begin to experience some of the pollution that is experienced by other parts of Canada where settlement is more dense and where there has been settlement over a longer period of time.
Interest in this question and the importance of the problem itself is indicated by the growing concern of various groups, in the first instance of the provincial governments and then of various agencies within the provinces. It is a matter which was discussed at the annual resources conference in British Columbia, where pollution is a serious problem in coastal areas at the present time.

It is held annually in British Columbia and has paid considerable attention to the increasing menace and danger to the purity of our waters. It was also a subject of considerable discussion at the "Resources for Tomorrow" conference held in Montreal from October 23 to October 28 last year. Anyone who has perused its most interesting and valuable reports will see the importance that was attached to the problem.
In that connection I wish to quote briefly from its reports. I should say it is not my intention to speak at great length because I want to give hon. members an opportunity to express themselves on this subject. This is a paper which was prepared by Mr. J. R. Menzies, chief, public health engineering division, Department of [National Health and Welfare, Ottawa. It was headed "Water Pollution in Canada by Drainage Basins" and in it he mentions:
A publication of the World Health Organization contains the following statement:
"When the forces of sanitary deterioration are considered, such as those that accompany increasing population density and industrialization, it becomes evident that the sanitary control of the environment is slipping backward. In spite of all of a positive nature that WHO and similar agencies have attempted to do, the world is probably in worse sanitary condition now than it was 10 years ago. The forces of deterioration have outstripped the forces of betterment."
It would be unfair to regard this as an accurate statement for all parts of Canada but it accurately portrays conditions in fairly extensive areas where pollution abatement and control are not receiving sufficient support from regulatory authorities and the general public.
He goes on to say, under a paragraph headed "Water use, and effects of pollution":
Water use may be thought of in several broad categories such as domestic, industrial, agricultural, power, navigation, wild life and recreational. The effects of pollution within these classifications vary widely.
Then he goes on finally to say:
Broadly speaking, the effects of pollution become a matter of general interest only when they are notoriously bad.
That is the unfortunate position, Mr. Speaker. People only become interested when the effects are notoriously bad. He went on to say something about conditions in the waters that are not affected to any great extent today:

The situation arouses public attention when a body of water becomes septic or when fish and wild fowl are destroyed in quantity. Because of modern water treatment methods, water-borne epidemics are infrequent although it is quite possible, even probable, that epidemics of non-fatal character go unrecognized as being water-borne. When tastes or odours develop in a municipal water supply due to pollution, they are usually of local interest.
That situation has been brought to my attention by one or two smaller municipalities in my constituency. This article continues:
Two conditions of increasing significance are related to the rapidly expanding use of synthetic detergents. Even with modern sewage treatment methods these detergents are not neutralized or destroyed to the degree that their effects are not recognizable. Because they contain elements such as phosphorus in the form of polyphosphate additives, it is suspected that they may be, in part, responsible for luxuriant growths of algae in the receiving waters.
That is a complaint I have had brought to my attention:
Complaints concerning algae are becoming more frequent. Tastes and odours may result from their decomposition and the cost of water treatment is increased.
Mr. Speaker, I mention this because not only have we been affected by the traditional pollution caused by municipal sewage, industrial waste and so on, but now we have this added problem of detergents. I think a good many housewives would be much wiser to return to the good old soap and water. However, in the past there has been some good work done in Canada in connection with this problem. At this time I wish to pay tribute to the work that has been done by the international joint commission as the result of co-operative effort between the Canadian and United States sections of the commission, co-operation between provinces and states which has been extended to the commission, in some cases municipalities and in other cases the industries that are causing the pollution complained of.
I think the first reference to the international joint commission on this question was made in 1913, but I think it was 1946 before any concrete references were made to the commission and their attention was directed to particular problems and particular studies.
I suggest that anyone who is interested in this subject should obtain a copy of this latest booklet issued by the Canadian section of the international joint commission entitled "Safeguarding boundary water quality. A co-operative effort between United States and Canada under international treaty", referring to the boundary waters treaty of 1909.
I mention this because it does offer a guide, as a result of experience, regarding the direction in which federal and provincial governments should go if this problem is

Criminal Code
to be met. Some excellent work has been done by provincial governments, agencies of provincial governments, in some instances by local conservation organizations and groups, and in a few cases by the industries particularly concerned with the problem. I think it is safe to say that experience proves the necessity for federal-provincial government co-operation and action if the problem is to be met properly in the near future.
That is the experience of Great Britain. In recent years they have had to revise their legislation with respect to water pollution and obtain the co-operation of the counties, the municipal authorities, and so on, and they are now-just think, at this late date-beginning to attack this problem in a manner that is producing some desirable results.
That has been the experience in the United States. The problem was left to the local authorities, and over the years the states made some piecemeal approaches to it. Now they have found from experience, however, that the problem can only be met as a result of co-operation between the federal government, the states and the local authorities.
In connection with this matter I wish to mention some recommendations that were made at the resources for tomorrow conference with respect to the problem of water pollution. I suggest that these recommendations should be considered by us all. The conference recommended the creation of a water pollution control division within the framework of the proposed national resources council composed of representatives of the 10 provinces. There was the further recommendation that there should be extensive research into the whole problem as it affects the rivers, lakes and streams of this country, and that there should be a national development fund set up to be used in this field as a result of co-operation between federal, provincial and municipal authorities.
Mr. Speaker, I have touched on the question in a rather broad manner. I dealt with this matter rather broadly to indicate the importance of even this first step. I do urge hon. members to indicate their interest in this problem and their determination to do something about it, even in this limited way, by supporting this very simple amendment to the Criminal Code.
In conclusion, I once again urge hon. members to support this legislation as one more small step toward the elimination of the evil of water pollution, a problem which has been discussed in this house and in the legislatures of this country since 1867. I think it is time now that we ended the talking and took action.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a real privilege to participate in this debate on Bill No. C-13 to amend the Criminal Code sponsored by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). He indicated that he sponsored a similar bill at the last session of parliament, and mentioned that it was identical to the bill sponsored by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) back in 1956, I think.
I had the privilege of moving the following resolution on June 9, 1958:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing a measure to provide by amendment to the Criminal Code appropriate punishment for the offence of water pollution.
The bill before us today is similar to that resolution. On that occasion I believe 20 hon. members from all sides of the house took part in the debate, and I think all of those who spoke supported the resolution. The hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken), in supporting the resolution expressed regret that it did not also include appropriate punishment for the offence of air pollution. I do not think air pollution is as widely scattered as water pollution, but it is prevalent in large industrial centres and is a real problem.
The matter of water pollution is of concern to all Canadians. I recall hearing a statement that, at the rate of pollution that was taking place, by 1980 there would not be a clean stream or river left in Canada. This situation is alarming. It has often been said that water is our most important natural resource, that it is more important than our minerals, oil, agricultural products, and the like.
Representing a Manitoba riding which includes all of lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba, and having my home at Gimli, a town on the shores of lake Winnipeg, I am very conscious of water pollution. Interprovincial rivers empty into lake Winnipeg. These include the North and South Saskatchewan rivers. Both these rivers originate in the Rocky mountains. We also have the Assiniboine river, which originates in western Canada. Then we have an international river, the Red river, which originates in the United States. These rivers are polluted along their way by raw sewage. Various towns and cities dump their raw sewage into these rivers, and they are also polluted by industrial wastes. This eventually entered lake Winnipeg, resulting in the pollution of part of that lake. In addition to having an adverse effect upon fish and wild life, this has also created problems for some of our summer resorts situated on both the east and west sides of the southern part of lake Winnipeg.

Water pollution is not a new problem. It has been discussed in this house on a number of occasions. As the hon. member who introduced this bill mentioned, a similar measure was introduced in this chamber in February of 1956. The hon. member for Prince Albert, now Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) speaking on the resolution he introduced in that year had this to say as will be found at page 1631 of Hansard:
In other words, the amendment which I am suggesting is to cover the general situation arising out of the pollution of interprovincial streams in Canada. In the case of navigable streams offences are created in so far as the Fisheries Act is concerned when anything in the nature of an effluent and the like is dumped into a stream and causes harm to fish; but in so far as interprovincial rivers are concerned, as the law stands today there is practical immunity for those who dump effluents into the river because of the wording of the section in question which permits wanton and wilful pollution of streams when there is no effect upon the health and comfort of the individual.
There are many examples of this, one outstanding example being the majestic Ottawa river which adjoins these parliament buildings.
I am sure all hon. members are familiar with the pollution problem caused by the discharge of sewage into the Ottawa river. The hon. member for Prince Albert also had this to say:
I believe that in the realm of God's richest bounty clean river water should have a high place and ought not to be allowed to be sacrificed to private greed or to wanton and wilful pollution. There is nothing today in the law to protect the public against wanton and wilful pollution by a small minority who for their own purposes contemptuously disregard the public interest in so far as interprovincial rivers are concerned.
This matter is of great importance for all Canada, because I think every province has some interprovincial river running through it. I recognize the urgency of the subject under discussion. I am also concerned about the heavy expenditure which will certainly be involved in solving this problem. The cooperation of individuals at all levels of government will be necessary if pollution is to be eliminated. The bill under discussion makes it an offence for the owners of industrial plants and oil refineries, or other persons, to discharge noxious matter into an interprovincial water thus endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public. This is a preventive measure. However, in order to correct existing conditions the installation of many filtration plants will be required. I believe financial arrangements will have to be worked out between all levels of government to this end, since the problem is one which is of enormous size.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Mc-Cleave) speaking on the resolution I introduced on June 9, 1958, had this to say as reported in Hansard at page 975:

I think it should also be pointed out to the house that one of the problems we are going to face in setting up this safeguard, and I hope we do, is a municipal one.
Many of the municipalities will find it extremely difficult to finance sewerage and other large undertakings. They have found these projects difficult in the past with the result that many of the growing communities-and I have in mind particularly those in Halifax and in the Montreal area-have tackled the problem in a piecemeal fashion. There is a widespread use of cesspools, which sometimes stay within limits but sometimes, unfortunately, do not, thus causing great difficulties to those downhill.
I think in proceeding on a resolution of this kind we must be very careful that we do not initially throw too great a burden upon the municipal authorities who are finding it difficult enough at the present time to raise the wherewithal to provide for their necessary services.
I agree with the hon. member for Halifax that many municipalities will find it difficult to finance these sewage treatment projects. The government recognized this at the last session of parliament when amendments to the National Housing Act were passed. Part VI B of the act deals with loans in respect of municipal sewage treatment projects and I should like to refer to that act for a few moments. Section 36F states:
In order to assist in the elimination or prevention of water and soil pollution in any municipality the corporation may, with the approval of the governor in council, make a loan to a municipality or a municipal sewerage corporation for the purpose of assisting in the construction or expansion of a sewage treatment project.
Then the clause goes on to outline the various conditions upon which such loans may be made. The act also provides some incentive. The following clause, clause 36G states:

It is extremely gratifying to be a supporter of this government headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the first government to take action with respect to water pollution.
At the resources for tomorrow conference which was referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) extensive discussion on the subject of water pollution resulted in several recommendations being made.
