speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to accept the invitation extended by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) of indicating the interest and support of the Liberal party with respect to the objectives sought to be achieved by this bill.
In his bleak expose of the problem the hon. member cited examples of water pollution, particularly in British Columbia. The examples he gave I feel could also apply to all parts of Canada. I believe that all hon. members on all sides of the house and from all parts of the country will accept and support the principles and objectives of this bill. It seems to me we should be careful to ensure
that our affection for and interest in the subject matter of this measure is not so excessive as to lead to our smothering the bill by talking it out. For that reason I propose to be extremely brief in my remarks.
On the order paper Bill No. C-13 is referred to as an act to amend the Criminal Code, and in parenthesis there appears the word "nuisance." That, to me, is a masterpiece of understatement. In my opinion the reference should be not to nuisance but to the sabotage of our natural resources.
I am sure hon. members in all parts of the house who live anywhere near water have been astonished and alarmed by the rate at which the water of our rivers is being polluted. I live in an area where water is extremely important. My home town of Sorel is situated at the junction of the St. Lawrence and Richelieu rivers. I have had ample opportunity to be alarmed by the increasing amount of pollution that is being experienced in both these rivers. I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that the federal government has certain responsibilities in this respect and can take certain steps to eliminate pollution. But if we wish to take effective measures to put an end to this sabotage there will necessarily have to be cooperation and understanding between federal, provincial and municipal governments. It is in the interests of each of the three levels of government to take immediate action in this regard.
Mention was made of the ways by which the water of our rivers is being polluted. Industrial waste and municipal sewage were referred to. However, there is another form of pollution which I feel comes directly under the responsibility of the federal government. I refer to pollution caused by ships emptying their bunkers before approaching large cities. This form of pollution is deadly. In the summer you can go along the St. Lawrence river and find all along the shore a film of oil about one quarter inch thick. Not only are our beaches contaminated by this deposit but the fish are affected and in our area the ducks are also gradually being killed off.
Another serious form of pollution is municipal sewage. The government introduced legislation to assist municipalities in constructing sewage disposal units but the cost is prohibitive and many municipalities are unable to purchase equipment. If we are to meet effectively the problem of pollution further assistance must be given the municipalities to help them assume their share of the work involved in preventing water pollution. As the hon. member for Kootenay-West said, the effective solution of this

problem will require co-operation among individuals, shipping companies, all levels of government and others.
I am not sure this bill will cover all aspects of the problem but I feel the house at this time should take an active interest in this matter. This is not the first time the subject of water pollution has occupied the attention of this house. As has already been mentioned the Prime Minister when sitting as a private member placed on the order paper similar motions. At that time he was keenly interested in having the federal government take the lead in putting an end to water pollution. Later, during the election campaign of 1957, the hon. gentleman had definite plans to bring pollution to an end. Speaking in Prince Albert as reported in the Prince Albert Herald of May 28, 1957, the Prime Minister said:
Speaking about water pollution, Mr. Diefenbaker said: "We will never build great cities in this country unless there is legislation to prevent pollution of water".
And later:
He told of the time he introduced a bill in the House of Commons which would provide for legal punishment of persons found contributing to water pollution. He promised that such legislation would be a major matter for consideration when "we form the government".
The party which is led by the hon. gentleman now forms the government but he has not as yet introduced legislation that would have the effect of putting an end to water pollution. The Prime Minister made a definite promise in Prince Albert. He cannot claim to have fulfilled that promise. I am not sure whether it is one of the 12 that have not been fulfilled, or whether it is one of the 70 general promises made in that period.
If water pollution was an important problem in 1957 is it not equally important in 1962 when the hon. gentleman is in a position to bring into effect legislation of the type about which he bragged in the election campaign? Water pollution is an even more serious problem now than in 1957. Every year there appears to be an increasing amount of pollution in the St. Lawrence and Richelieu rivers and I have no doubt this is true of rivers throughout Canada.
If the government is sincere and if the Prime Minister when he makes a promise intends keeping it, I can see no better way for the government and the Prime Minister to demonstrate sincerity and good faith than by taking action with respect to this bill or by introducing an even more comprehensive measure. I do not believe there is one opposing voice with respect to the objectives that are set out in this bill. I do not believe there is one person in the house who does not realize that our rivers are being rapidly
Criminal Code
contaminated and that our game and our fish are being rapidly destroyed. If everyone feels that this is so I cannot understand why action is not taken on legislation such as this.
In order not to talk this bill out, Mr. Speaker, I will now resume my seat.

Just a minute. The hon. member spoke about not wanting to talk the bill out. We have other members who wish to speak on it. I wish to deal with the bill itself right now.
The bill itself talks about interprovincial waters and that is all this bill deals with. It makes provision for dealing with a definite situation in interprovincial waters. Interprovincial waters are the rule on the prairies. I would ask the hon. member for Kootenay West what interprovincial waters there are in British Columbia? I am not going to talk about the Peace river. We have political pollution there. I am talking about the majority of the waters in British Columbia. What about Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick? This bill does not even give a time when it is supposed to come into effect. As I said, I think the hon. member for Kootenay West has been led down the garden path by his own well developed sense of humour. Although the Prime Minister put this in, it is not the solution to the problem. The problem is a real, vital and important one for the people of this country. I refer to water pollution.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext: We did not say it was the solution. We said it was one thing we could do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION

All right. I am glad that the hon. member for Kootenay West has come to the point where, no matter how far in the past the Prime Minister has made a suggestion, he automatically accepts the entire validity of whatever has been said and will follow John. I know he is coming very close to this party, just as his leader may be coming closer to the official opposition. We will welcome the hon. member for Kootenay West whenever he wants to come over to this side of the house. However, if he had read the speeches of the Prime Minister, he would know what he was aiming at at this point.
I say that the government has been taking action to correct water pollution and that

it has been doing so in a way which has been effective. I say that the government will continue to take action to correct it. However I do not see that this bill will do it. For instance let us consider a river such as the Saskatchewan and the hundreds of small communities which lie along that river. Immediately this bill comes into effect every one of those communities is under a fantastic penalty. The record is clear. The hon. member for Selkirk made it clear that these communities, one after the other, are within the limits of their financial resources moving in a way in which they have never moved before in order to take care of this problem of water pollution. This is the way in which it will be done. This is the way in which that particular problem will be cleaned up. However, there are many others in existence. There is the problem of disposal of industrial waste. This material can be even more of a peril than sewage, particularly to fish life.
I wanted to answer the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, Mr. Speaker. I also wish to say that the members who speak on this bill are not trying to talk it out. We are trying to bring intelligent criticism to bear on the bill. We recognize the problem. We also recognize and give credit for what the government has done. I suggest to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres that his speeches would be far more effective if they were a little bit more reasonable and if they recognized a few of the things that have been done. Having done that, let him then make his constructive criticism, if he has any.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to enter this debate briefly. Os do all hon. members in this house I am sure most thinking Canadians realize that pure water, our greatest natural resource,

will in a few years be in a position of critical shortage. I should like to compliment the hon. member who brought this bill before the house, because I think it is a most timely one. I commend his common sense in bringing in one that was originally sponsored by the right hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I should like to suggest to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) that if, as he says, the Prime Minister has suggested that his government would be dealing with the problem, it will be dealt with. I say to him that after all we have anywhere from another eight years to 16 years in which this present government can still deal with it. Hence it should be well taken care of in good time.
I should like to put on the record this fact. It seems to me that under the British North America Act rivers-and of course, that is where our pollution is-are the responsibility of the provinces. In 1960 the committee on mines, forests and waters took a very careful look at this question. The Hon. Alvin Hamilton, speaking on Tuesday, March 22, 1960 had this to say:
South of the 60th parallel, the responsibility to develop streams and waters is primarily that of the provinces. They must plan to develop domestic and industrial supplies of water. Irrigation, power, flood control, abatement of pollution.-
This is what this bill covers.
-recreational uses of water are the provinces' prime responsibility. The federal government, in turn, has a responsibility to protect and develop inland fisheries, to protect the navigability of streams and, by virtue of its jurisdiction in agriculture, a responsibility to ensure an adequate supply of water for agricultural purposes. In the international field, the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that boundary waters are not polluted to the detriment of health.
I became interested in this particular subject many years ago when living on the banks of a beautiful river in northern New Brunswick, the Restigouche. I saw how that river, famous for its Restigouche Atlantic salmon, was being polluted by industrial waste and by the raw sewage of the towns on its banks. Then, a few years later when I went to live on the St. John river, the Rhine of America, again I saw the same situation. This river, one of the most beautiful in our whole country, has now reached a point where youngsters can no longer swim in it. It is now, completely impossible to drink water from the St. John river unless it is chlorinated. Pollution has reached the point where even the fish population seems to be dying off.
What is happening? First of all, pollution from a number of pulp mills and other plants, 26207-1-53
Criminal Code
raw sewage from cities such as Fredericton and Edmundston. About a year ago provision was made by this government to aid municipalities in the construction of sewage treatment plants. Unfortunately, no city in New Brunswick took advantage of that legislation. However, when the camp Gagetown project was built-it now has 11,000 people-provision was made for a sewage treatment plant, the only one of its kind in the whole province. As I have said, the river is being slowly but surely killed by industrial wastes, by bark from pulp and from raw sewage.
I was most interested a few nights ago in watching a television program in which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier-Lasalle (Mr. Pratt) participated. He pointed out how that portion of the St. Lawrence river and the beautiful Ottawa river were being destroyed. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Campbell) was telling me a few minutes ago that the river beside which he lives in Ontario, the Sydenham, has been almost completely polluted.
Where does the solution to this problem lie? It seems to me that legislation will have to be passed that will force industrial plants to purify their waste material. In the committee that I mentioned earlier, there was a representative of the Cities Service Oil Company who told us his company had established its own filtration plant. After their wastes had been treated, the water was almost pure enough to drink. I felt at that time it was a much better idea for a company to spend part of its profits in this way than in most of the ways in which companies do spend money on advertising. What about our own beautiful St. John river? For many years it has been urged by capable and thinking men in my part of Canada, especially Mr. R. A. Tweeddale, general manager of the New Brunswick electric power commission, that there should be a St. John river authority to deal with all problems such as this. This particular idea has been strongly supported by our local newspaper, the daily Gleaner. I think it is most commendable. I think that is the point that will rapidly have to be reached if we are to save the fish that are in our rivers and if we are to prevent our rivers becoming open sewers. I commend the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) upon his introduction of this measure before the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken on this subject before and I imagine that my views are well known to the house. I agree completely with

Canadian National Railways the hon. gentleman who has sponsored this bill and I am convinced that his objectives are of the highest. I agree in principle that the bill is serving a good purpose. There is, however, one section of the bill to which I would take exception. I refer to the section which speaks of a person who discharges any noxious waste product into a river, stream or other water any part of which is interprovincial which has the effect of endangering lives or safety, rendering himself guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine of $25,000. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this might lead to more trouble than the bill is intended to prevent. As I have said in a previous speech on this subject, the making of such an offence a criminal offence would, in effect, make a poor soul who flushed a toilet responsible for a $25,000 fine.
Speaking on behalf of my own city of Dorval which has been making provisions steadily, I might say that my municipality is very well advanced with plans. We have chosen a site for the construction of a sewage disposal plant. Certainly many municipalities have expressed great appreciation of the legislation introduced by this government in 1960 which provided for loans, as hon. members know, covering two thirds of the cost of those plants at a very low rate of interest over periods as high as 50 years. Provision is made also for an outright grant of 25 per cent of the cost of any work which is done before the end of March 1963. I understand that the city of Vancouver has already submitted plans for a scheme covering something like $7.5 million. I understand the city of Ottawa also is taking advantage of these grants.
Nevertheless, I think basically the responsibility for ensuring that we do not suffer from the pollution of our waters is a provincial responsibility. I think the federal government has done what it could, that it is now up to the provinces to see that sewage disposal plants are built and that advantage is taken of legislation which is already on the statute books.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE BETWEEN MATANE AND STE. ANNE DES MONTS, QUE.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Balcer- Mr. Martineau in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize and to provide for the construction and

operation on behalf of Her Majesty of a line of railway in the province of Quebec, between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts, a distance of approximately 57 miles; to provide also that the governor in council shall pay to the Canadian National Railway Company an amount equal to the cost to the said company of constructing the railway line (including the cost of survey of location and the cost of acquisition of the land required for the railway line) not exceeding in any case the sum of $16,100,000.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

Mr. Chairman, this house has before it not only one of the most important measures, but one that is vital for the survival of the Gaspe peninsula. I am quite moved as I rise to take part in the debate on this resolution and to act as the voice of a population which has always fought loyally and sincerely, not asking for handouts, but for a project which is essential to the development of an area which has for so long been ignored and neglected.
Mr. Chairman, Jacques Cartier landed at Gaspe in 1534. Some 400 years later, in 1952, Gaspe Copper Mines Limited, a subsidiary of Noranda Mines Limited, founded the first mining town on the north shore of the Gaspe peninsula. The town was called Murdoch-ville for the president of the Noranda Mines Company, Mr. J. William Murdoch. Over 1,200 people find work there and we are at one in acknowledging this attractive little town as the queen of the Gaspe peninsula.
Mr. Chairman, do you not find it amazing that it took more than 400 years for a mining corporation to settle in the Gaspe peninsula and make the people benefit from the immense resources placed there by Divine Providence? Around Murdochville, corporations own lands just as rich, if not richer, than those owned by the Gaspe Copper Mines. And just to prove my point, let me mention some of them: the Federal Metal Corporation, owned by East Sullivan and Consolidated Mines Limited, Miller Copper, Dubuis-son Mines Limited, Lake Opawica Mines Limited, Macdonald Mines Limited, Thompson Mines Ltd., Copra Mines Limited, Christie Base Metal Limited, etc.
All those companies were waiting for the construction of the railway to start operating their mines.
The known mineral resources on the north shore of the Gaspe peninsula are as follows:

90 million tons of yellow copper; 40 million tons of red copper; 20 million tons of zinc; 6,400,000 tons of chrome; 4,500,000 tons of aluminum oxide; 23,125,000 tons of manganese, asbestos, nickel, gold and silver.

Mr. Chairman, after hearing about the mineral wealth of the Gaspe peninsula, can there be anyone in this house-including even that hon. member who does not seem to take any interest in the problems of Quebec-can there be anyone in this house who cannot say down in his heart that it is unbelievable that such a rich area of our country should have been deprived so long of appropriate means of transportation and that such a hard working population should have suffered so long from that situation?
Hardships are not unknown to the people of the Gaspe peninsula, and if it is true that one is all the nobler for his hardships, the people of the Gaspe peninsula are surely the noblest people one can find.
The Gaspe peninsula is also quite rich in forest resources. Following a survey conducted by Mr. L. P. Peloquin, who was chairman of the industrial committee of the Matane chamber of commerce, we find in his report the following information. In the area to be served by the Matane-Ste. Anne des Monts line there are: 129 saw mills in operation; 41 26207-1-53i
Ungava transport operates a daily ferry service for passengers and freight between Ste. Anne des Monts and Seven Islands. After a few years of operation this service has developed to such an extent that the first ferry had to be replaced by a larger one.
It is interesting to note that in 1958, over
8,000	people used that fast, regular service from Ste. Anne des Monts to travel between the Ungava district and the industrial centres of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. Since 1956 this figure has gone up considerably, and once the railway is built this service will expand and promote great economic development between the north shore and the Gaspe peninsula.
Speaking of the first ship which provided a regular service between Ste. Anne des Monts and Seven Islands, I must say that this ship which gave excellent service is operated by Ungava transport whose president is Mr. Jourdain, a Gaspe businessman.
The first ship which undertook that service in 1958 could carry 50 passengers, three automobiles and 100 tons of cargo. In 1960, it was replaced by a new ship with a total capacity of 100 passengers, 35 automobiles and 800 tons of cargo. That year it transported 14,000 passengers, 3,000 automobiles and 7,000 tons

Mr. Chairman, I should now like to illustrate the development possibilities of the Gaspe district.
I have already mentioned the numerous mines which are to be found in that part of my riding. In that connection, I should like to read to the house a letter which was sent to Mr. Roland Gagnon, a young industrialist of the Gaspe peninsula who is largely responsible for the construction of the railway between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts. Mr. Chairman, I would ask those who are not convinced that a railway is necessary in the Gaspe area to listen carefully to this letter which should certainly make them change their minds:
September 9, 1960
Mr. Roland Gagnon,
Cap Chat, Que.
Dear sir:
Further to our telephone conversation, I am pleased to confirm the following information.
Solbec Copper Mines Limited is a new subsidiary which is developing copper and zinc deposits in the Black Lake district, in the eastern townships. It is expected that the annual production will amount to nearly 20,000 tons of copper concentrate.
We do not fail to realize that the Gaspe copper refinery might be the proper place for treating our ore, if that plant were not completely isolated by a lack of communications. We believe that it is unfortunate for the district of Gaspe and also for eastern Quebec, that such a lack of communications more or less occasions treatment of our concentrates outside this country, that is in the United States or in Europe. We shall welcome the building of a railroad across the peninsula for many reasons such as have been mentioned earlier today: the eventual development of some zinc and lead deposits of the Federal Metal Corporation; mining possibilities in the Gaspe area and in eastern Quebec, which are still practically unexplored.
We remain at your disposal for further information if required.
Sincerely yours,
East Sullivan Mines Limited,
Andre Beauchemin, Secretary Treasurer.
Mr. Chairman, may I point out the splendid part played by Mr. Pierre Beauchemin in the development of mining in the province of Quebec.
As far as the forest industry is concerned, I also would like to read a letter addressed to the chamber of commerce of Gaspe North, at Ste. Anne des Monts, attention of Mr. Fernand Leblanc, secretary. Incidentally, I


would like especially to commend this chamber of commerce for their outstanding work and the magnificent support given to the project. I quote the letter:
To the chamber of commerce of Gaspe North, Inc. Ste. Anne des Monts, P.Q.
Dear Sirs-
Attention): Mr. Fernand Leblanc, secretary.
It has been brought to my attention that you were making representations in order to have extended the railway line which ends at Matane along the north shore of Gaspe, and our company supports your efforts for the following reasons, which I shall explain briefly.
For the past three or four years, the use of wood waste as raw material for pulp and paper has developed to such a degree that it is now in our mutual interest that our industry and the saw mills get together-we being buyers of such waste and the saw mill operators being suppliers of wood fibre which it is becoming more and more difficult to obtain.
In your area there are several saw mills which would be interested in transforming their waste into fibre for our mill here in Three Rivers. There are, among others, the following companies: Jas. Richardson Company, Tourelle Lumber Co., and A. Couturier et Fils with whom we have negotiated. However, we always had to face the transportation problem. These three mills would have about 35,000 tons of waste to sell immediately and, once this market is established, this quantity could easily be doubled in your area.
The construction of a railway from Matane, with reasonable freight rates, would solve the transportation problem and would create in that area a market which would be beneficial both to the buyer and the seller.
We hope that your efforts to obtain this railway will be successful and we are anxious to know what comes out of your negotiations.
Yours very truly,
St. Lawrence Corporation Limited,
L. L. Wetmore,
Manager.
According to economists, the railway between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts must accompany and precede progress. If it comes after, it is late, and the consequences are felt by the economy and the industry, and unemployment runs high among our good Gaspe families.
On March 17, 1949, Mr. S. M. Fairweather, vice president of the Canadian National, made the following statement in a speech delivered in Toronto:
A railway must he considered in relation to the economy of the country, for it is essential to the prosperity of the state and it gives birth to wealth. Those of us who live in the big cities might not see it, but the miner, the lumberman, the fisherman and the farmer are fully aware of the usefulness of a railway. We discover every day new resources and new fields of activities where development is made possible by the railway which is as important to the state as arteries to the human body.

Mr. Gordon, president of the Canadian National, voiced the following opinion:
In a country like ours where distance is a main factor in the cost of products, one cannot consider the development of our natural resources without thinking of a railway.
The Canadian National Bank, in its monthly report for February, 1959, had this to say:
Why defer the construction of the Matane-Gaspe
sector, which would serve such an interesting area-
On page 12 of Commerce et Communication of November 28, 1961, we read the following:
Will Gaspe North have its railway at last? The transactions relating to the sale of the railway between Mont Joli and Matane are nearing completion, and it seems that the project of extending this line up to Ste. Anne des Monts is being seriously considered in government circles in Ottawa. It is easy to understand the importance of that railway improvement in the Gaspe peninsula since Ste. Anne is the ferry terminal to Seven Islands. For the past fifty years, everyone has been beating around the bush, always shelving that project, and this piece of news is greeted with great enthusiasm by present and future industrialists and businessmen of the area and also by the population.
The Gaspe peninsula is one of the least developed areas of the province. Yet its industrial potential does not. warrant such a situation. The main weakness in the regional organization seems to be the lack of main lines of communication, such as railways. However, it appears that the federal government, at long last, has concerned itself with the famous Gaspe railway project which is to be announced shortly.
Everyone knows that the extension of the railway from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts has been, for the last 20 years at least, the subject of numerous representations on the part of members of parliament and people of that part of the province.
I also wish to refer to a letter, which is not recent, addressed to Mr. Gagnon, promoter of the project, on March 30, 1959 by Canon J. A. Saint-Laurent, chaplain, and I quote:
Dear Sir:
I see in L'Action Catholique of March 28, 1959, that you are actively interested in the extension of the railway from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts.
Why not as far as Gaspe?... While I was in charge at Cap Chat, from November 18, 1911...
Note the date.
...to October, 1912, temporarily replacing the good father Dufour, who had died suddenly, the question of this extension had been mentioned for a long time, but... as far as Gaspe.
The question was basically about the possibility of getting there through Ste. Anne from the north. A survey had been made and it could be easily done.
There was a persistent rumour to the effect that the railway from Matane would rather be extended along the river, running across the good lands given by Quebec as a grant to the company. There was thus a question of private interests involved.
I was aware of that rumor and able to meet with both the engineers from Ottawa and Quebec, at an
Canadian National Railways appointed date, in the Cap Chat rectory. The discussion was soon on the extension of the railway from Matane to Gaspe, through Ste. Anne.
By the end of the evening, the federal engineer stated:
"I had not yet completed my survey when I was summoned to Ottawa. All I had then was an approximate layout and reported it was impossible to reach Gaspe through Ste. Anne." The first report was therefore cancelled.
I arranged with the parish priest of Ste. Anne to have the leading parishioners of both political parties meet at the rectory and this was done. We also had with us four of the most interested members of parliament.
All agreed to have a third survey made, complete, this time-in order to clear up the matter. But what about the costs? All county councils will be called upon to pay for those costs on the basis of their population. The devoted Mr. Emile Cote, a merchant of Cap Chat, agreed to pay for those who would not keep their pledge. All county councils readily signed the ready-made form.
The survey was made. The report showed a complete possibility. The costs would amount to $15,000; which were paid by Ottawa.
Now that we have Murdochville do you not think, sir, that you stand a better chance? You have the ready co-operation of Baie des Chaleurs, on account of the numerous industries which would be established in the Gaspe peninsula.
Good luck in your fine work for the development of our Gaspe peninsula.
Devotedly yours in Our Lord Canon J. A. Saint Laurent, priest, Chaplain.
Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Charles Marcil indeed referred to the Gaspe railways, at the time. He is a former member for Bonaven-ture. The Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux took the floor in the house and asked for the construction of railways in the Gaspe peninsula. My predecessor also talked about that here in this house, and demanded a railway. And I shall always remember what he said in closing his speech: "My dear colleagues, the fate of the Gaspe peninsula is now in your hands."
And I can well remember the words of the bishop of Gaspe, Mgr. Ross, asking for a railway. I recall also the words of Mr. Taschereau who was then premier of Quebec. He used to say and repeat exactly the same words: "It is up to you, gentlemen of the Canadian National Railways, to think of the Gaspe peninsula."
Mr. Chairman, I have put forward the needs of my area, in this house, and I think it was my duty to do so as member for that district, but I have always done so, regardless of petty politics, because the interest of a province and of a constituency must be placed above political meanness.
Mr. Chairman, I also remember very well that here in this house the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has

Canadian National Railways very often blamed the Prime Minister for his trips across the country. I should like to remind him that in 1960 the Gaspe peninsula had the great honour of welcoming for the first time in its history the leader of the federal government. The Prime Minister wanted to see for himself what were the needs of that area and get acquainted with the people who have suffered for so many years and who are only asking to be treated fairly. He met those people, he offered his help and I am proud to say that two years after this historic trip to the Gaspe peninsula, we are getting what we have been asking for for 300 years, that is, a railway in the Gaspe area.

I wish to thank the house. I should not want to abuse the time at our disposal, but it seems to me that there is no abuse in devoting a few minutes to an area which well deserves it and for which I have always done and will always do the best I can.
Mr. Chairman, before closing, I should like to express my thanks, first to the most humble people, the workers, the fishermen of my province, those who, in 1957, sent me here to this house to plead a worthy cause, not only that of the railways, because a railway in itself is of little meaning, but that of the general development of a region recognized as one of the richest and most promising.
I wish to thank most sincerely the chambers of commerce of my constituency. I need not refer to the numerous resolutions sent to me by chambers of commerce, municipalities and economic organizations requesting this railway or asking me to work on their behalf. There are many such resolutions, as you can see. I should like to show you here requests sent to me by the people of Gaspe to ask me to plead for them.
I thank the chambers of commerce for their help. Without them, I could not have worked so efficiently. The chambers of commerce of my constituency are free from all political ties. I feel sure that all hon. members agree with me that we get much encouragement in our work from these organizations, in the way of information and advice, which is something I appreciate.


I also thank the clergy of Gaspe for the constant support it has given me. I thank all our industrial leaders. My thanks also to all the municipalities, to all public bodies.
I should also express my very special thanks to the Minister of Transport, the sponsor of the bill, who will always be remembered in Gaspe.
I should not want to overlook his predecessor, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), who was also interested in this improvement when he was minister of transport.
I should also like to thank my colleagues, the members for Matapedia-Matane, Rimou-ski, Bonaventure and Magdalen Islands (Messrs. Belzile, Morissette, Grenier and Keays) who have seconded my efforts.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, I should also like to thank the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who stated this afternoon that his party would support this project. Indeed, I am sure all hon. members will vote in favour of this resolution.
I do not intend to linger on this subject but I should like to refer to certain statements made by the hon. member for Port Arthur this afternoon. While he stated that this project was not within provincial but rather federal jurisdiction, the hon. member wondered why a construction project concerning the Gaspe peninsula had been chosen. Well, if the hon. member had better knowledge of history, he would be aware of the fact that the Gaspe peninsula is the oldest part of this country and that this construction project of a railway line was contemplated long before the other projects he mentioned. Gaspe is one of the richest regions with an outstanding mining and lumbering potential.
The hon. member should also know-and that is not my fault-that the Gaspe people never quit and will never rest till the projects they have suggested are carried out.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a word of thanks to the press, because since the question of building a railway in the Gaspe peninsula has come up, the Quebec papers have given it an excellent coverage which I am sure has largely contributed to the realization of this project.
Finally, I should like to thank everyone.

I know that my hon. friend has always been interested in that project-

Anne des Monts, in order to extend the one that already exists between Mont Joli and Matane, a project which is about to be carried out, goes back many years. As for myself, during the 1958 electoral campaign, I often had the occasion to talk about that project, not to promise the railway, but rather to state that I was committing myself to work for its realization.
That is why, as soon as I came to the House of Commons, in 1958, on May 23, to be precise, when taking part in the debate on the speech from the throne, to prove my firm intention to work on that project, I made the following remark, which can be found at page 411 of the official report for May 23, 1958:
Before concluding these remarks, may I be allowed to point out to hon. members that the area commonly called the Matapedia and Gaspe valley is part of Canada, that the people of this vast and recent section of the country pay taxes to the federal government and contribute to the building up of our homeland, and therefore are entitled to consideration on the part of the federal government.
It was an area that was very much neglected by the former administration which, fortunately, now is sitting on the other side of the house.
In the field of public works, I strongly support the project of my colleague, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English), providing for the extension of the Mont Joli-Matane railroad to Ste. Anne des Monts.
This being said, Mr. Chairman, I would now like to suggest to the house that the question of the construction of a railroad in the Gaspe peninsula has been discussed for a long time. The project has been a topic of current interest for 75 years. The figure may seem enormous, but let me quote an editorial of La Minerve for Monday, September 12, 1881. That article is doubly interesting for it deals not only with railway lines, but it would be a timely topic in the Gaspe peninsula
Canadian National Railways even today though it could be called an historic document. May I quote the editorial:
The Gaspe peninsula is a special part of French Canada the same as Magdalen islands or the former Acadia (which is part of Canada since 1867). It is hardly known in the province of of Quebec proper. Formerly it was a special governorship which had very few contacts with the governorships of Quebec, Three Rivers and Montreal which constitute a compact homogeneous group. In our times, contacts have become more frequent but have never reached the degree of intimity and perfect uniformity which marks the contacts between the other districts of the St. Lawrence.
The Gaspe peninsula and its people are still in our opinion a sort of far away colony of separate brethren, quite like the Acadians.
That is due first of all to the distance-the Gaspe region is a hundred leagues away from Quebec city_and to the lack of communication through part of those one hundred leagues.
The Gulf and Intercolonial Steamers line brought the Gaspe peninsula closer to Canada and the rest of the continent. But a seaway is not too important and the railway is still far away from the real Gaspe region. Men who came from central regions to settle in those far away places and to dedicate themselves to the development of the region-like Dr. Fortin and Dr. Robitaille-have done more than all that to make us known to the Gaspe people and to acquaint us with them.
Besides, as long as railway communications are not further extended, that is as long as one cannot travel by train right to Perce, the head of the Gaspe peninsula, we cannot expect that those relations will improve substantially.
It would be beneficial, however, to the people of the Gaspe peninsula if its isolation should come to an end. They would have everything to gain especially if they were to develop a liking for agriculture in addition to engaging in fishing, an inexhaustible industry, but which today makes only employers wealthy and keeps workers in a state of serfdom and poverty.
And now, Mr. Chairman, coming back to a more recent period and especially to the project now under discussion, I should like to tell the house that two former Liberal members for the Gaspe peninsula, that is the member for Gaspe, Mr. Langlois, and the member for Matapedia-Matane, the late Philias Cote, were interested in the same project. Incidentally, reading Hansard I came to the conclusion that it was a pity that the government of that time did not find it appropriate to consider their request and accede to the wishes so aptly brought forward by these two government members.
By doing so, the Liberal government not only deprived those two members of the credit they would have gained through their joint efforts, but also, by neglecting to face the problems, it deprived the Gaspe peninsula of the means of transportation it was entitled to, contributed largely to delaying its economic development and caused considerable harm to the population of the Gaspe peninsula as a whole.

Poor Mr. Cote, how wrong he was; unfortunately for him, his government waited so long that he died in the meantime and never had a chance to see Mr. Graydon's prediction come true, namely that it was necessary that the Conservative party take office in order that the demands of those two members be satisfied.
Unfortunately, too, for the Liberal party, which always had counted on Gaspe as a vested riding, because its red army was seen to collapse and lose all the seats they retained on the lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, the two events I just mentioned, that is, the premature death of Mr. Cote, and the defeat-or should I say say the downfall-of the Liberal party are of secondary importance compared to the considerable damage to the whole population and, more particularly, to the people of Gaspe, through the carelessness and neglect of the former government.
In order to give a brief history of the project, may I point out that the fathers of confederation were so keen on obtaining the assent of the maritimes to their confederation project that they had to promise them a railway which would link them to the great central provinces of the country.
It was in fulfilment of those promises that the Inter-Colonial was built, and that is why the railway, instead of following a straight line, turns off at Mont Joli toward the maritimes, and the north shore of the Gaspe peninsula is isolated.


It is therefore patent that private initiative alone made the Gaspe peninsula what it is today.
Industrialists, businessmen, farmers and fishermen, who are handicapped by inadequate means of transportation, nevertheless made some progress.
Mr. Chairman, this is a long peninsula which extends for 150 miles between the St. Lawrence river, to the north, and the Baie des Chaleurs to the south. It is covered with mountains and forests and has a central plateau.
On the south side of the peninsula, a C.N.R. branch line runs along the Baie des Chaleurs shore from Matapedia to Gaspe. Therefore, the north shore of the peninsula is deprived of railways, to the exception of the section from Mont Joli to Matane, which is served by the Canada Gulf Terminal Railway.
The main industries of the peninsula are lumber, fishing and mining.

This will result in an upsurge of the economic life of the Gaspe peninsula.

At last the railway.

For his part, the mayor of Matane, Mr. F. A. Gauthier, said he was very glad of the project, in the sense that it will represent an improvement on the transportation system in the Gaspe peninsula.

The project could not he more serious, since it is part of the federal government's program for this session. It is the fulfilment of a promise which Mr. Diefenbaker made personally during the 1957-58 campaigns.

fair claims of the citizens of the Gaspe peninsula, who, under Liberal regimes, had acquired the rather unenviable title of the eternally forgotten people.

The Gaspe peninsula undoubtedly deserves full consideration from the federal government. It is common knowledge that for years now there has been an exodus of the people from Gaspe precisely because natural resources are not sufficiently developed in that area. Therefore, the resolution introduced today by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) is most timely.
I trust that the hopes raised by the construction of this new railroad in the Gaspe area will come true and that we will finally see the establishment of new industries in that peninsula. Let us hope that thanks to the present government, the Gaspe peninsula will no longer be looked upon with contempt and considered as an underdeveloped area of the province of Quebec as it was in the past. That has never been my attitude since I feel that the people from Gaspe form the very root of the population of the province of Quebec. I would even say that Gaspe is somewhat the birthplace of many a Montreal resident because a great number of people from Gaspe settled in the metropolis.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) indeed asked me two or three questions this afternoon.
The first was about the Canada and Gulf Terminal railway. Well, I am glad to remind the house that during the years 1900 to 1910-I can't say exactly what year, because I do not have the necessary document here, but I think it was in 1903 or 1904-the railroad in question obtained a federal grant. At that time, and as a condition of that grant, the government had required the railroad to guarantee a right of way to any other railroad which would claim one in the future.
This means that all the Canadian National Railways has to do to obtain a right of way on the Canada and Gulf Terminal railway is to make an application to the board of transport commissioners to obtain it and have the terms thereof set.
The hon. member has also asked me if the government had studied the possibility that the local mining companies might use the piggy-back system to allow faster transportation of the various ores extracted in the hinterland of the Gaspe peninsula.
Those are technical problems that will be. solved by the authorities of the Canadian

Canadian National Railways National Railways. I admit that his suggestion has much value but, all the same, I cannot tell him if the Canadian National Railways will adopt that system or not.
Mines in operation and those which may become active in the future will undoubtedly have to ship their ore by the C.N.R. and it would be to their advantage to use piggyback facilities. However, since that railroad will be operated by the C.N.R. for the federal government, it will be up to the officials of the company to take a decision in that respect.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier asked a purely irrelevant question. In fact, he asked why the federal government does not help Quebecair which serves that area. As the hon. member knows, the government has considered recently various means of helping Quebecair and certain proposals have been submitted both to the federal government and to the air transport board but they have been turned down. However, I want to state here tonight that there is no doubt that this company will receive the same treatment as the other air lines. If some circumstances should arise and if the government should consider that it is its duty to assist that company, there will be no hesitation. In short, that company will always be treated on an equal footing with similar companies.
Before I close my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank all those who took part in this debate and particularly the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English) who spoke with deep feeling. It is no wonder he was moved since this project has been his life-work, as he said so eloquently. In fact, he succeeded in voicing his own feelings and he really moved us by his warm observations about his region, his county and all the speakers who took part in the debate.
I also thank the member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Belzile) for his most thoughtful contribution, and I am very obliged to him particularly for having mentioned the names of several people in his constituency and the surrounding areas who have lent assistance, exerted pressure on the government and supplied all the necessary information to implement that project which I am sure will have most beneficial effects for that part of the province of Quebec and Canada.
As a matter of fact, the Gaspe area is extremely interesting; it is one of the most colourful parts of the country. It is unfortunate that all its great natural resources remained undeveloped, and that the population of that area was condemned to eke out a living by fishing.

speechtext:
I should like to add a few remarks to the short speech I made last night. The purpose of the proposed legislation is to amend section 13 of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act, chapter 242, R.S.C., 1952 to increase the limit of the borrowing power of the authority to $345 million from $335 million.
Section 13 of the act was amended by 7-8 Elizabeth II, chapter 9 (1959), to increase the power to borrow money from $300 million to $335 million. This provision states as follows:
13. The authority, with the approval of the governor in council, may, from time to time, borrow money from Her Majesty or otherwise for the purposes for which it is incorporated, but the aggregate of the amounts borrowed under this act and outstanding shall not at any time exceed three hundred and thirty five million dollars.
Section 25 of the act provides that the Minister of Finance with the approval of the governor in council, may, from time to time, make loans to the authority to the extent only that parliament has authorized such loans to be made in a fiscal year.
When, in 1959, an amendment to section 13 of the act was proposed to the house on

January 16, it was intended to cover certain estimates which were in excess of the amount of $300 million which had been set in previous measures. This time the amount being asked for is needed to meet some current commitments for outstanding work and contractors' claims which will exhaust the authority's present borrowing power. The additional $10 million will be needed for the remaining contractors' claims, land settlements, construction works including the completion of the Cornwall north channel bridge, a floating crane and certain remedial works, landscaping and wharf improvements.
On the last occasion when my predecessor brought in a similar amendment, an additional amount of money was asked for. This time there is simply a change in the general amount required. The only reason we are bringing this amendment forward is because these claims have been settled and the present borrowing power of the authority has been exhausted. We feel that this additional amount requested would be enough to cover the commitments and pay these claims.

There will, of course, be no objection from this side of the house so far as this additional expenditure is concerned, but I should like to take this opportunity to do three things. First, I should like to say a word in commendation of the St. Lawrence seaway administration in so far as traffic on the seaway is concerned. I have not before me the latest figures and I doubt even if they are public, but 1 have those for November 1961 and they indicate that 23 million tons passed through the St. Lawrence canals. For the Welland canal, the figure was 30 million tons. In the first case, that is almost two and a half times as much traffic as there was before the opening of the seaway, which certainly represents a tremendous increase. In the second case, traffic on the Welland canal is 10 million tons more than that which existed before.
It is true the Welland canal has not reached the 40 million tons anticipated by the tolls committee, neither has the 30 million tons anticipated for the St. Lawrence canal been reached. However, I will say that in the three years during which the canal has been in operation the volume of traffic has been extremely encouraging. What is even more encouraging is the fact that the smaller vessels, the 14-foot vessels, are fast disappearing from the seaway in favour of larger carriers such as 20,000 and 25,000 ton carriers, many of which are being built. This means that in the long run the smaller vessels will disappear in favour of the larger ones. It may
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act well be that when the tolls advisory committees of the seaway meet again to establish what the amount of the tolls should be the estimate of traffic will then have been reached because of the increased carrying capacity of the larger vessels. I am not at all dismayed by the fact that the tonnage has not reached the anticipated maximum. I am rather pleased by the fact that the tonnage has increased tremendously from what it was prior to the seaway.
At this point the house will probably permit me to place on the record what was said by Mr. R. J. Rankin, president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority in a speech delivered at Dearborn, Michigan, on January 15, 1962 in dealing with this and similar matters. He said:
Within the authority, we do not share the opinions of those who have sought-through relating the actual revenues of the past three years to the estimates of the tolls advisory committees- to demonstrate that the seaway has made a poor showing and that there are serious doubts it will meet the objectives that have been set for it. As we see it, there is no sound basis for such thinking, nor, as of now. for any proposals which relate to the need of relief through lower interest rates, extensions of time or increased tolls.
These are matters which relate directly to 1964 when the seaway entities are required to present to their respective governments an appraisal of their financial position.
Another significant paragraph from the speech reads as follows:
In the three year period of its operation, the authority believes the seaway has given a good account of itself. It is quite true, as has been emphasized by outside analysts from time to time, that tonnages and revenues have not reached the levels originally estimated by the tolls advisory committees. However, to use this as an argument to condemn the work of the committees is, we believe, both unrealistic and premature. It may well be that the upward curve of tonnages and revenues is not as sharp as was forecast but this may or may not be significant in the long range view. Who is to say, for instance, that in the next, say five or six years, the tonnage volume and revenues will not reach and even exceed the levelling off point set by the committees. And it is the degree to which it exceeds this levelling off point which will determine whether or not the seaway pays off as planned.
As it has been agreed by both the United States development corporation and our own Canadian seaway authority I think we must await the time when there will again be an analysis of the whole position.
The minister made reference to the additional amount that was required and the purposes for which it was required. When one looks at the list of expenditures he can immediately come to the conclusion that these are natural expenditures. For instance, I remember that the predecessor of the minister rose in the House of Commons because of demands that were made from the

St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act shipping fraternity that access wharves to the Welland canal should be built. These were built by the seaway authority at a cost of $4.5 million. It is only natural that authority should be sought to include that sum. The minister, of course, said at that time in answer to a question I put to him, that those would be paid for by an item in the estimates of the Department of Transport. That decision was altered and the St. Lawrence seaway authority is charged with that responsibility.
Then there is the north channel bridge at Cornwall which costs a substantial sum of money. There is also the landscaping that was done in the St. Lambert area. There are settlements for the expropriation of land, expropriations which had been made a long time ago but which had not yet been determined either through negotiations between the parties or by the courts. In addition, of course, there are claims that had been made by contractors.
The claims are nothing out of the ordinary. Claims were made against the power authority in substantial amounts. Claims were also made against the Ontario Hydro and against the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, the United States entity, in substantial amounts; and so it is not out of the way that claims should be made against the Canadian entity. I see that according to the list the sum of $1,800,000 is required for that amount.
There is also a crane that is being purchased at a cost of $1,200,000. All of these expenditures total approximately $10 million. Having regard to the long term period over which the St. Lawrence seaway will operate I do not think this is extraordinary, particularly having regard to the interest during construction which on a project such as this represents a tremendous amount.
By an arrangement made between the seaway authority and the Department of Finance the interest during construction does not begin until 1963. I may be mistaken as to ,the years but I believe it was in 1959 and 1960 that the St. Lawrence seaway authority had to borrow funds to pay substantial amounts for interest during construction. In one case the total was $19 million. They took $3 million of that from their own revenues and borrowed the remaining $16 million.
May I conclude by expressing this thought. I observed in the press mention of the fact that Mr. Gordon Murphy, chief engineer of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, is to retire on March 1 next. I should like to pay a

tribute to Mr. Murphy. He was responsible in no small measure, together with many others, of course, not only for the preparation of the plans and specifications of the seaway but also for the engineering work during the first years of the operation of the seaway.
Mr. Murphy is a man of vast experience. He was port manager in Montreal and served with the national harbours board in Ottawa for many years. He was selected because of his qualities as an engineer and his qualities as a man of tremendous integrity. Everyone who has come in contact with him will agree that Gordon Murphy was a dedicated worker. He took no holidays during the time I served with the seaway and I am informed he took very few holidays since I left. His industry, his humanity and his qualifications as an engineer lead me to believe that the success of the seaway was due in no small measure to his efforts. I should not wish to allow this measure to pass without expressing a word of commendation concerning not only an outstanding public servant but an engineer of tremendous capacity.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORITY TO BORROW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have little to say for or against the principle of the bill. As hon. members may be aware, various members of this party including the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) over the past two or three years have placed on the order paper a number of questions relating to the St. Lawrence seaway, the contracts and various expenditures that have taken place. Many of these questions were prompted by a certain scepticism about the nature of the contracts and the efficiency with which they were carried out.
The hon. member for Assiniboia is not present this evening, but I trust that when the bill is before the committee hon. members who have expressed an interest in this matter will have an opportunity of examining in some detail the purposes for which this extra money is required in the light of the replies that have been received from the Department of Transport in response to questions about the St. Lawrence seaway authority.
The only point I wish to make about the seaway is this, and perhaps it is in some conflict with what was said by the previous speaker. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) spoke about the success of the seaway. I wonder whether it has really been a success so far? At the western end of the seaway-great lakes waterway we have seen that the growth predicted has thus far not fully materialized. I wonder, therefore, whether the

seaway is not another example of our having oversold ourselves on a grandiose scheme? I wonder whether the St. Lawrence seaway is not another example of the kind of grandiose scheme where we oversell ourselves. On the one hand we build ourselves up on the St. Lawrence seaway and the tremendous impact it was going to have on the growth of our inland seaway in relationship to the west. In fact, the progress in terms of the increased shipments has not really been that much, at least as reflected in the upper lakes.
The other point about the seaway that comes to mind is this. In the area in which it has been more properly advantageous- and I am thinking there of the situation in the lower lakes and the passing of the iron ore traffic from Quebec into the steel making heart of the country-there is the fact that we have this immensely strong pressure group that is ranging the country from one end to the other led by a man of considerable ability-I refer to Admiral Mainguy-campaigning for the abolition of tolls and, at a minimum, campaigning for an approach to the St. Lawrence seaway that will see that no additional burden is put upon the shipper.
My point here is that, as a result of the arrangements made with the United States, the cost of the seaway remains a considerable charge upon the shipper, particularly with respect to the Welland canal. From the fact that we have ranged on one side or the other, the people who are charged with the provision of the service, and the carrier, who are going to be unhappy about the tolls, and the people in the west who are somewhat disappointed at the growth consequences of the seaway, I wonder why we have to be so enthusiastic as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) still seems to be about the so-called wonderful success of the St. Lawrence seaway system.
The question that can undoubtedly be put is this: Do you consider the St. Lawrence seaway to be a failure? May I say that it is a gigantic engineering success but that it has been a very costly undertaking on the part of this nation, although perhaps one that was fitting at its time. We will welcome the opportunity of supporting the measure that will go towards clearing up any indebtedness that remains. However, I think it is over-optimistic to conclude that this has been the great cure-all for many of the economic problems of the St. Lawrence seaway-great lakes basin.
It is also apparent that a residue of harsh and contradictory feelings still exists within our neighbour to the south among various
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act regional groups with regard to the development of the seaway. We have some groups contending that the United States government should build its own canal past the Niagara escarpment because of the dissatisfaction with the present arrangements. Perhaps one cause of the present feeling is that this would put more properly within United States hands where it belongs control of the traffic going through there. On the other hand, on the eastern seaboard and in the south, there are vigorous groups related to different shipping lines and different shipping ways who are very much against what they consider to be the subsidization that is still going on with regard to the seaway. Given this complicated pattern in the United States and the general situation in Canada with regard to the same contention that still exists about the potential, we shall look forward to hearing in greater detail in the committee the reason for this extension in the expenditures.
The point that might be made more efficiently by the hon. member for Laurier would perhaps be that one of the reasons for disappointment in the growth factor that we have noticed with regard to the western end lies in the coincidence that as the St. Lawrence seaway began to operate, it also went along with the change in government.

speechtext: I know this is a familiar argument that comes from the Liberal benches. I am unable to see the matter in these terms, Mr. Speaker. I should be obliged to express the opinion that whether or not the Liberals were in power, the St. Lawrence seaway would be in the position in which it is today of not meeting its projected income and of falling a good deal short of what was projected for it in terms of effects, both direct and peripheral, on the economy of the country.

I should just like to add a word of comment on the last two speeches. I listened to what the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said. I noticed that he spoke about making up our minds whether this is a success or a failure. May I say that the time to make up our minds in deciding whether it was to be a success or a failure was before it was built. We have it now.
I was interested in what the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said. After all, he has had a special opportunity to know its operations. I find it reassuring to hear his words of confidence. They were not words of exaggeration but nevertheless were words

of solid confidence. While we have this bill before us it seems to me that it would be wise for us to get to know the project better than we know it now. As for myself, I must confess that I have had a feeling that the project is falling somewhat below the expectations which had arisen in the decades we talked about the undertaking. It was natural that expectations should rise very high. It seems to me we should know how matters are working out. I have no doubt the minister can show this while the bill is before the house, and let us have the real picture as to what is happening and what the chances are of its paying its way in any reasonable time. That is what interests me and I believe it is what interests the people of Canada generally.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING PAYMENTS TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to indicate my support and the support of this party for the second reading of this bill. We are now discussing the principle of the bill. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to make a clarification of a statement which I made on Friday when we were discussing this measure at the resolution stage. At that time I said, as reported on page 741 of Hansard for February 9, 1962:
We now have in Newfoundland two classes of foresters, those who served in world war I and are veterans and entitled to benefits under the veterans charter and those who served in world war II who are not veterans-
When the minister was speaking yesterday, as reported on page 773 of Hansard, he took exception to these remarks and, in particular, he took exception to my use of the word "now". I should like to make it clear to the minister and to the house that I in no way intended to blame the government for anything that happened prior to 1957. Certainly, all down through the years since 1949 when Newfoundland became a part of Canada, we have had the situation in which the foresters who served in the Canadian army or Canadian units, were regarded as veterans; the foresters who served in the Newfoundland forestry units in world war I were regarded as veterans. The status of those Newfoundlanders who served overseas in the forestry emits during world war II has been in doubt. Their services have not been recognized for the purposes of pension or for any other reason. By implication, we have refused to accord them the status of veterans. When I used the word "now", what I was pointing out was that we are doing something in this act which had not been done previously. So long as we withheld a decision, then those Newfoundlanders who served in the forestry units in world war II could not say that we had decided about their status one way or another. We had not made any pronouncement or we had not pronounced any verdict as to what we considered their status to be. We have done so now, and we have this written into a bill which is going to go on our statute books.
I refer particularly to clause 75 of the bill which says that, for the purposes of this part, "civilian" means certain things, and then it goes into a whole list of categories as to what constitutes a civilian for the purposes of this act. Under paragraph (a) it says that a person who served at sea in a ship of Canadian or Newfoundland registry during world war I or world war II for a period of at least six months shall be a civilian under this act.

Then, we go further and under paragraph (g) we say that a person who served with the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit in the United Kingdom during world war II for a period of at least six months and who contracted to serve with that unit for the duration of the said war, shall be classed as a civilian. We have classified them. Then, to make sure that there is no doubt about it, we have written into another part of the act, clause 70, subclause 2, which states that in applying the act to the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952, schedule A, established for the purpose of this part, the word "veteran"-I ask hon. members to note this-the word "veteran" where it appears therein shall be read therein as "civilian". This is the point to which I intended to refer the minister. This is what is happening if this legislation is passed. I used the word "now" and perhaps I was a little premature in anticipating the passage of this bill, although we know that with the government's majority it will go through. I hope we can still appeal to the minister to reconsider this decision.
May I call it ten o'clock?
